Paris Sept. 2.—Premier Daladier made plain to the Chamber of Deputies at to-day's historic Session that France would fight to aid Poland unless Germany halted "aggression".

The premier told the Chamber:

"There is no Frenchman marching toward the lines who marches with hatred of the Germans, but he marches knowing the very existence of his country is at stake!"

Without formally declaring war, Daladier bound France's fate to that of Poland by declaring:

"Is there German-Polish war? No. There is a step in Hitlerian German efforts to dominate the world."

However, Daladier left a slight hope for peace.

"Even at this moment, if the Germans leave Poland, if they stop their aggression, France will not refuse efforts for negotiations. If representations are tried again, we again are ready to associate in them."

"Gentlemen, today it is France that commands," he said, concluding among the cheers of the chamber.

Because so many of the teachers
were members of its faculty and
were unable to attend their classes,
the Henderson high school suspend
ed for the day. Three grades at
Junior high were also without teach
ers, who roomed in the building, but,
by doubling up and with the aid of
substitutes, that school continued to
operate. Some of the teachers who
work in the other schools were also
unable to attend their classes, but no
others were forced to suspend for the
day.


Fire Chief Cooper Ellis said the
old structure burned almost like tin
der, and that many of its timbers ap-
peared to be almost solid lightWood.
Nearly the entire second story and
roof were burned away, and the first
floor was badly damaged by water
and smoke, and slightly by fire
While the building was not a total
loss, many who viewed the ruins to-
day wondered if it were worth the
extensive and costly repairs that
would be necessary to restore it.


Superintendent E. M. Rollins, of
the city-county school system, said
the loss was at least partially in
sured, but he did not know imme-
diately the exact amount of protec-
ton carried.


The fire appeared to start in a rear
bathroom, where stove was burn
ing. The entire structure was heat
ed with stoves, as it did not have a
heating plant.


The building had some Is to 18
rooms, and was the home of the 10
teachers who lived there. They had
rooms and also were furnished board
at the teacherage.


Some twenty years ago the city
school board purchased the property
from private interests for some So
600. Nearly that much more was
spent on the large frame building
to condition it for the accommoda-
ton OF the teachers in the city
schools, though by no means all of
them had rooms there.


Many Of the teachers were forced
to flee the burning structure in scant
clothing. Some were seen walking
about the place after the fire was
brought under control clad only in
their night apparel and coats, and
wearing bedroom shoes. They had
lost part or nearly all of their per-
sonal belongings.


Numerous citizens came to their
aid and took them to their homes for
temporary quarters until more de-
finite arrangements can be made.
The fire started just before the break
fast bell, and none of the teachers
had had their breakfast when they
were ousted from their quarters by
the flames.


The city schools have only little
more than month yet to run of the
present school year, and it is expect
ed that more definite arrangements
can be made by the start of the new
school term in the fall.

BY the Associated Press. -


MINNEAPOLIS, Dec. 30.- Suspension of Finland's war debt payments was urged last night by former President Hoover in an address, marking the first large meeting in the Northwest for Finnish relief.


Mr. Hoover, in charge of the national Finnish relief fund drive, told a crowd estimated at 500 that never there was a case in history where a creditor should show his own decency by suspending payments our Nation should do it now for Finland.


The former President stressed that Finland alone of its debtor nations has paid every installment and that, despite that country's present troubles, it made one of its payments to the United States only two weeks ago.


New Low for Civilization.


"Civilization struck a new low with the Communist attack upon peaceful Finland" Mr. Hoover asserted. "It is a sad day to every decent and righteous man and woman in the world. Whatever its terrible vicissitude may be, the soul of this intrepid race cannot be crushed by an oppressor, for Finland—the people of Finland—will not die."


Emphasizing that the fear of invasion by armies hangs over billions of people in the Old World, Mr. Hoover said "There is the sickening fear of fire and destruction to innocent people from the air. There is the dread fear of hunger and famine. There is the fear of pestilence. And with these four horsemen of the Apocalypse now comes the fifth, even as dreadful. That is the fear of all liberty loving people of the sweep of Fascism, Nazism and their blood brother, Communism, with their armed aggression against free men. With them comes destruction of all the world has builded of justice, of law, of freedom to worship, of freedom of thought."


Gov. Moore Raps Russia.


JERSEY CITY, Dec. 30 (P.)—Calling for support of the Finnish relief fund, Gov. A. Harry Moore of New Jersey last night called Russia a "bloody, Godless monster."


"There is glory" he declared at rally, "in the fact that they (the Finns) are hurting back this bloody, Godless monster. Pray, as you do, that the Finns may be successful.


The Russians consider ethics only as they best fit their own scheme of things.


It is fitting that New Jersey should come to the aid of the Finns, who were among the pioneer settlers of this State in 1888."

see vases of flowers droop before they
can be carried into the living room
This is sign of lack of care A
bouquet should last for several days.
remaining fresh and attractive. To
do this, the flowers should be cut in
the evening or early morning when
the stems are full of water. Imme-
diately upon cutting place them in
vessel of cold Water-covering as
much of the stem and foliage with
water as possible without wetting
the blossoms Allow to stand in the
cold water for several hours. This
hardens the stem. After this hard
ening process most flowers will with
stand heat and drafts without wilt
ing.


When you buy evergreens from
the nurseryman remember that he
has kept them clipped to keep the
growth bushy and compact You
too, should clip them if their growth
is to continue thick and healthy in
appearance. March and September
are the months in which to prune.
